messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 73

# Dr. Linh's Careful Distance

Dr. Linh has been practicing emergency medicine for twenty-three years. Her colleagues describe her as unflappable—the kind of physician who moves through chaos with purpose, who remembers patient names and asks about their children. She arrives early, stays late, and has trained three generations of residents. But for the past eight months, something has shifted.

It started on a Tuesday evening in the emergency department. A man came in agitated, bleeding from a laceration on his forearm. Dr. Linh was suturing the wound when he suddenly became aggressive, accusing her of poisoning him. She tried to de-escalate, speaking quietly in her practiced, calm voice. Security was called, but before they arrived, the man lunged at her, striking her face and neck repeatedly. Other staff pulled him away. She has a small scar above her left eyebrow that catches the light when she turns her head.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The other injuries have not.

Dr. Linh returns to work two weeks later, as she had always imagined she would. She is a doctor; she understands trauma. She has treated hundreds of assault victims. She knows the statistics, the recovery trajectories, the importance of returning to routine. But in the department now, her body operates on a different frequency than her mind intends.

She finds herself positioning her body differently during patient interactions—angled toward the door, never fully turning her back. When patients raise their voices, even in pain or frustration, her heart rate spikes. She has become hypervigilant in a space she once felt in control. The fluorescent lights seem harsher. The sounds of the monitors and alarms, which once formed the comfortable backdrop of her professional life, now feel threatening. She startles easily.

At home, her husband notices she no longer relaxes on the couch beside him in the evenings. She sits on the edge of the cushion, her body tense. She has stopped going to the community center where she used to swim. The thought of being in a space where she cannot see all the exits makes her stomach clench. She lies awake most nights, and when she does sleep, she dreams of hands reaching for her face, of being unable to move. She wakes with her heart pounding, gasping as though she has been underwater.

The intrusive moments come without warning. A patient with similar features to her attacker will walk in, and suddenly she is back in that moment—the shock of being vulnerable, of her expertise and authority meaning nothing. Her hands shake slightly as she continues the examination, hoping no one notices.

Dr. Linh finds herself making excuses to avoid certain shifts. She volunteers for administrative tasks, something she never did before. She has begun to wonder if she can continue in emergency medicine at all. This thought terrifies her more than the assault itself. Her identity has been built around this work, around being the steady presence in crisis. Now, she feels like a fraud—a physician who cannot manage her own nervous system.

She tells no one at work. She has confided only in her husband, and even then, she minimizes. She is fifty-one years old and has spent her entire adult life in control. The idea of being labeled as traumatized, of needing help, of admitting that an eight-minute encounter has fundamentally altered how she moves through the world—this feels impossible.

Yet she comes in each shift, watching herself from a distance, wondering when the person she was before will return.
